title: Symmetry
shortDescription: Lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry and symmetric letters/figures.
genZNote: Fold it, flip it, rotate it — symmetry is just 'does it still look the same?'

sections.heading: Lines of Symmetry
sections.body: A line of symmetry divides a figure into two mirror-image halves. Rotational symmetry order is the number of times it looks the same in a 360° turn.

sections.heading: Symmetric Letters
bullets: Vertical-axis symmetry: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y.
Horizontal-axis symmetry: B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X.
Point (rotational) symmetry: H, I, N, O, S, X, Z.

sections.heading: Applications
sections.body: Questions ask to complete a figure so it is symmetric about a dotted line, count lines of symmetry, or identify the mirror partner. Check each point's distance from the axis; mirror images are laterally inverted (see Non-Verbal Reasoning for mirror/water images).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Symmetry tests whether a figure maps onto itself under reflection or rotation.
keyFacts: Square has 4 lines; rectangle 2; circle infinite.
H, I, O, X are symmetric both ways.
Parallelogram has no line of symmetry.

commonTraps: Do not count a rectangle's diagonals as symmetry lines.

sources.name: Standard competitive-exam reasoning reference (R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning)
